CHIEF COMPLAINT
Persistent shortness of breath and worsening cough with greenish sputum.
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Lysander Fairfax returns for follow-up two days after his last visit. He reports that despite initiating Levofloxacin, his respiratory symptoms have not improved. He continues to experience significant shortness of breath, particularly with exertion, and his cough remains productive with greenish sputum. Mr. Fairfax mentions that he has noted intermittent fevers and increased fatigue, which have further diminished his overall well-being. He describes his wheezing as persistent, particularly at night, and states that he is using Albuterol more frequently, approximately every 2 hours, without significant relief.
He expresses concern regarding his lack of improvement and is anxious about the possibility of a more serious underlying condition.
REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General - + fatigue, + intermittent fevers, - weight loss, - chills, + night sweats. Pulmonary - + persistent productive cough with greenish sputum, + increased wheezing, - hemoptysis. Cardiac - no chest pain, - orthopnea, - paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Gastrointestinal - no nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Musculoskeletal - no joint pain. Neurological - no dizziness or headaches.
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: - Blood Pressure: 130/76 mmHg - Heart Rate: 80 bpm - Respiratory Rate: 28 breaths/min - Oxygen Saturation: 75% on room air.
General: The patient appears fatigued and is in moderate respiratory distress, using accessory muscles to breathe.
HEENT: No nasal flaring; oropharynx clear, no signs of dehydration.
Lungs: Marked wheezing on auscultation; decreased breath sounds bilaterally; prolonged expiration with notable rhonchi; crackles audible throughout lung fields.
Cardiac: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs or gallops; peripheral pulses intact.
Extremities: No edema; no tenderness on palpation.
ASSESSMENT
1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation, likely complicated by a bacterial pneumonia given the persistent greenish sputum and lack of clinical improvement on Levofloxacin. 2. Consideration for hospitalization given worsening respiratory status, persistent hypoxemia, and increased work of breathing. 3. Congestive heart failure remains stable; no signs of fluid overload.
PLAN
1. Admit Mr. Fairfax to the hospital for further evaluation and management of his COPD exacerbation and possible pneumonia; initiate intravenous Levofloxacin 750 mg daily. 2. Order a repeat chest X-ray to evaluate for new infiltrates or progression of pneumonia. 3. Start supplemental oxygen therapy to maintain saturation above 92%. 4. Continue oral Prednisone 20 mg daily for inflammation management; consider increasing dosage if no improvement is noted within 48 hours. 5. Consult Pulmonology for further assessment and management of his respiratory condition. 6. Reinforce patient education regarding the importance of adherence to treatment and recognizing signs of respiratory distress.
DISPOSITION
Mr. Fairfax was admitted to the hospital for further evaluation and management of his respiratory condition. He was informed of the need for close monitoring and potential interventions. A multidisciplinary team approach will be utilized to optimize his care and address any complications that may arise during his hospitalization. He was advised to communicate any changes in his symptoms promptly and to participate in discussions regarding his treatment plan.
